unit.title: Water, food and your body
unit.summary: Hydration, fuel, heat and altitude: how the body behaves on a climb.

lessons.title: How much water
lessons.objective: You can estimate water needs for a hike and read early dehydration signs.

payload.prompt: Water for four hours of moderate hiking?

explanation.correct: About half a liter per hour is the classic starting point, so roughly 2 liters.
explanation.incorrect: Needs vary with heat and effort, but half a liter per hour is a sturdy baseline.
explanation.sayThisLine: "About half a liter an hour, so two liters for this one."

payload.prompt: Which sign means you are dehydrated and should drink?

options.text: Your urine is dark yellow or brown
Your urine is clear and pale

explanation.correct: Dark urine means your blood is more concentrated because you are not drinking enough. A pale, clear stream means you are well hydrated.
explanation.incorrect: Urine color is the fastest check. Dark yellow or brown signals dehydration; pale is good.
explanation.sayThisLine: "My urine was dark, so I doubled my water."

payload.prompt: You are two hours in on a hot day. Which of these suggests dehydration?

options.text: Your mouth is dry and you feel thirsty

explanation.correct: Thirst and a dry mouth are early signals. Drink before you are very thirsty, and sip often instead of waiting.
explanation.incorrect: Tired legs come from climbing, not dehydration alone. But thirst is the body's call for water.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I felt thirsty, so I knew it was time to drink."

payload.prompt: When is the best time to drink water on a hike?

options.text: Only when you feel very thirsty
Regularly throughout the hike, before thirst hits
All at once at the end of the hike

explanation.correct: Small sips throughout the hike keep you ahead of dehydration. By the time thirst is strong, you are already behind.
explanation.incorrect: Waiting until lunch or until you are very thirsty lets dehydration build. Sip often and early.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I sip every twenty minutes, not just at lunch."

payload.prompt: On a hot day, how does your water need change?

options.text: You need less water because you sweat less
You need more water because you sweat more

explanation.correct: Heat makes you sweat more to cool your body, so you lose water faster. You may need 50 percent more on a hot day.
explanation.incorrect: Heat increases sweat loss, not decreases it. Plan for more water on hot days.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Desert heat means I carry a lot more water than on a cool day."

lessons.title: Making water safe
lessons.objective: You can compare ways to treat backcountry water and name what they stop.

payload.prompt: Match the water treatment method to what it does.

pairs.definition: Pumps water through a membrane that blocks parasites and bacteria
Iodine or chlorine dioxide kills pathogens but does not remove all toxins
Heat kills parasites and bacteria, but is slow and fuel-heavy
Ultraviolet rays kill microbes, light and fast but needs batteries

distractorDefinitions: Letting water sit in the sun overnight

explanation.summary: No single method is perfect. Filters are fast and common. Chemicals are light. UV is trendy but needs power. Boiling works anywhere.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I use a squeeze filter, it's light but can freeze."

payload.prompt: What is giardia?

options.text: A parasite that causes severe stomach illness
A type of plant in clean streams

explanation.correct: Giardia is a microscopic parasite from animal feces in water. It causes severe cramps and diarrhea days or weeks later.
explanation.incorrect: Giardia lives in natural water and causes a nasty illness. Clear-looking water can carry it.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Clear water still has giardia. I've seen the hospital bills."

payload.prompt: You see clear, cold stream water. Is it safe to drink without treating?

options.text: Yes, clear cold water is always safe
No, treat it first. It can carry giardia and other parasites

explanation.correct: Clear water can carry giardia and other parasites. Clarity does not mean safety. Treat all backcountry water.
explanation.incorrect: The clearest streams carry invisible parasites. Treating all water prevents illness weeks later.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I filter everything. Even the pretty streams."

payload.prompt: What can a typical water filter remove?

options.text: Most bacteria and parasites, but not viruses or toxins
Only makes the water look better
Only removes visible bugs and leaves

explanation.correct: Most filters trap bacteria and parasites but not viruses or chemical toxins. In U.S. backcountry, that is usually enough.
explanation.incorrect: Filters are good at parasites and bacteria but not perfect against all viruses or pollution.
explanation.sayThisLine: "My filter stops giardia and cryptosporidium, which are the main worries in most places."

lessons.title: Salt and the water trap
lessons.objective: You can explain why plain water alone can be dangerous on long hikes.

payload.prompt: What happens if you drink lots of plain water without salt or food on a six-hour hike?

options.text: Nothing, more water is always better
Your brain can swell from diluted blood sodium, causing confusion and nausea

explanation.correct: Drinking only plain water without salt dilutes your blood sodium. This can cause dangerous swelling of the brain.
explanation.incorrect: Hyponatremia happens when plain water overfills your cells. Eat salty snacks or use electrolyte drink mix.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Chugging plain water all day isn't safe. Salt matters."

payload.prompt: Hot day, six hours out. Which drinking plan is safest?

options.text: Sip water and eat salty snacks
Chug plain water, no food or salt
Water plus electrolyte mix or sports drink

explanation.correct: Salty snacks or electrolyte drinks with water replace both fluid and salt. This keeps blood chemistry balanced.
explanation.incorrect: Plain water alone risks hyponatremia. Eating or drinking electrolytes prevents it.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I drop an electrolyte tab in one bottle every hot day."

payload.prompt: You are three hours into a mountain hike on a hot day. You have drunk two liters of plain water. Now you feel dizzy, a bit nauseated, and your head feels odd.

situation.narrative: You started early and planned a six-hour hike. The sun is intense. You brought four liters of water and trail snacks (nuts, cheese, jerky) that you barely touched.

facts.label: Food eaten
facts.value: Barely any, just a granola bar

options.label: Drink more water to flush it out
options.consequence: More plain water worsens dilution and makes dizziness worse. Your symptoms could become serious.
considerations: Plain water is the problem, not the solution
Dizziness and nausea suggest low sodium
More plain water makes it worse

options.label: Eat salty snacks and sip water slowly
options.consequence: Salt and food replace what plain water depleted. Your symptoms should improve over the next hour.
considerations: Salted nuts or jerky bring sodium back
Slow sips of water prevent more dilution
This fixes the problem, not just the symptoms

options.label: Turn back and descend to the car immediately
options.consequence: A safe choice if symptoms get worse. But trying salt and snacks first gives you the best chance.
considerations: Descending is not wrong if you feel bad
But mild symptoms often improve with snacks
Only descend if symptoms worsen after eating

payload.expertNote: Hyponatremia is rare but serious. The hint is plain water alone on a long hike plus symptoms of disorientation. Snacks and slower water fix it.
payload.sayThisLine: "I felt dizzy and ate some salted jerky. It helped."

payload.prompt: What are electrolytes in the context of hiking?

options.text: Salts like sodium and potassium that your body needs
Nothing you need to think about

explanation.correct: Electrolytes are essential salts your body loses in sweat. Replacing them keeps your blood chemistry safe and your muscles working.
explanation.incorrect: Electrolytes are minerals, mainly sodium and potassium. Sports drinks, salted snacks and even broth replace them.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I add electrolyte powder to my water on hot hikes."

lessons.title: Fueling the climb
lessons.objective: You can estimate calories per hour and pick sensible trail food.

payload.prompt: You are hiking steadily uphill for four hours. Roughly how many calories will you burn?

explanation.correct: Hiking burns roughly 350 to 500 calories per hour depending on pace and terrain. Four hours is around 1,400.
explanation.incorrect: The rate varies, but three to five hundred calories per hour is typical for hiking. Steeper or faster burns more.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Hiking burns about four hundred an hour, so I snack throughout."

payload.prompt: How should you eat trail snacks on a six-hour hike?

options.text: One big lunch in the middle
Small snacks every hour or so
All at once at the end
Do not eat, it slows you down

explanation.correct: Small, frequent snacks keep your energy steady and prevent bonking. A big lunch in the middle leaves gaps where you feel weak.
explanation.incorrect: Snacking every hour beats a single large meal. Your body burns fuel continuously, so supply it continuously.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Snack every hour, not just at lunch."

payload.prompt: Good trail food is {{quality}} and {{portable}}.

explanation.correct: Trail snacks pack lots of calories without weighing much, and they do not spoil or crumble in a pack.
explanation.incorrect: Good trail food is dense (nuts, bars, jerky), not light and fluffy (chips, popcorn). It has to survive jostling.

payload.prompt: Which of these is a good trail snack?

explanation.correct: Nuts, bars, chocolate, jerky and dried fruit are all great trail snacks. They are calorie-dense, shelf-stable and they pack well.
explanation.incorrect: Good trail food is calorie-dense and does not spoil. Mix salty, sweet and fatty for variety.
explanation.sayThisLine: "Tortillas and peanut butter is the best trail lunch."

payload.prompt: Which of these is NOT a good trail snack?

explanation.correct: Fresh greens bruise, wilt and spoil. They also do not have many calories for the weight.
explanation.incorrect: Trail food needs calories, durability and lightness. Lettuce fails all three.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I bring dried fruit and nuts, not fresh stuff."

lessons.title: Hitting the wall
lessons.objective: You can spot bonking early and know how to fix it.

payload.prompt: What is bonking?

options.text: Bumping your head on a low branch
Running out of energy, feeling weak and slow
A loud sound on the trail

explanation.correct: Bonking is hitting the wall: your glycogen stores are depleted and you feel weak, shaky and irritable.
explanation.incorrect: Bonking is an energy crash from not eating enough. You get slow and cranky.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I bonked at mile eight. Forgot to eat."

payload.prompt: Which of these is a sign that you are bonking?

explanation.correct: Bonking feels like a wall: weakness, mood changes, confusion and even tunnel vision. Eat and rest.
explanation.incorrect: Bonking is an energy crash. It brings weakness, mood shifts and sometimes strange symptoms.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I started getting cranky and slow, so I knew I needed to eat."

payload.prompt: Five hours into an eight-hour hike. You are getting weak, slow and irritable. Your legs feel like lead.

situation.narrative: You had breakfast at six AM and grabbed a quick snack at mile two (three hours ago). You have not eaten much since, and the terrain is getting steeper.

facts.label: Snacks eaten since breakfast
facts.value: One granola bar, at hour one

options.label: Push on to the finish, you are halfway done
options.consequence: Another hour of weakness makes you slower and more irritable. Hiking on empty is dangerous and miserable.
considerations: Weak muscles make mistakes
Low energy clouds judgment
Finish without eating is a recipe for trouble

options.label: Stop, eat snacks and rest for 15 minutes
options.consequence: Calories and a brief break restore your energy and mood. You finish strong in another 45 minutes.
considerations: Eating fixes bonking within 15 minutes
A short break helps more than you expect
Three miles is nothing with fuel

options.label: Turn back to the trailhead
options.consequence: A safe choice, but eating and resting would get you to the finish. Only turn back if eating does not help.
considerations: Turning back is safe but unnecessary
Food and rest usually fix bonking quickly
Only bail if symptoms worsen after eating

payload.expertNote: Bonking is predictable: you did not eat enough. Snacks restore energy within 15 minutes. Always carry more snacks than you think you need.
payload.sayThisLine: "I ate a few hundred calories and felt like a new person."

payload.prompt: The best way to avoid bonking is to:

options.text: Eat one big meal at the start
Do not eat anything, it slows you down

explanation.correct: Small, frequent snacks keep your energy steady all day. They prevent the crash.
explanation.incorrect: Snacking every hour beats any other strategy. Steady fuel beats big meals or going without.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I snack every hour now. Never bonked since."

lessons.title: When heat turns serious
lessons.objective: You can distinguish heat cramps, exhaustion and heatstroke in plain language.

payload.prompt: What are heat cramps?

options.text: Painful spasms in the legs, usually from salt loss and dehydration
Stomach pain from eating bad food

explanation.correct: Heat cramps are sudden, painful muscle spasms, usually in the legs. They happen from sweat loss and electrolyte depletion.
explanation.incorrect: Heat cramps are a sign of salt and fluid loss. Stop, rest, drink water with salt or sports drink.
explanation.sayThisLine: "My calf suddenly cramped, so I sat down and drank some electrolyte mix."

payload.prompt: What is heat exhaustion?

options.text: Fatigue, weakness, nausea and possibly fainting from heat stress

explanation.correct: Heat exhaustion is the step before heatstroke: weakness, dizziness, nausea and cool, clammy skin.
explanation.incorrect: Heat exhaustion means your body is overheating. Move to shade, drink water and cool off. It is serious.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I felt dizzy and weak on the hot trail, so we sat in the shade and drank water."

payload.prompt: What is heatstroke and how is it different from heat exhaustion?

options.text: Confusion, hot dry skin and loss of sweating: a medical emergency
The same thing, just a different name

explanation.correct: Heatstroke is a medical emergency: the person is confused, stops sweating and has hot, dry skin. Call for help immediately.
explanation.incorrect: Heatstroke is when the body's cooling system fails. Confusion and dry skin are the red flags. Descend and get medical help.
explanation.sayThisLine: "We started early because the canyon is dangerous by noon."

payload.prompt: Two PM on a canyon hike. Your friend is slowing down, looks pale and says she feels dizzy and sick.

situation.narrative: You started at eight AM and have been hiking steadily in a narrow canyon with no shade. The air temperature is 92 degrees F.

options.label: Keep hiking to the car, it is only two miles
options.consequence: Without rest and shade, heat exhaustion can worsen. Two miles in this heat could trigger heatstroke.
considerations: Symptoms mean she is overheating
Continuing without rest is dangerous
Heat exhaustion can become heatstroke fast

options.label: Stop, rest in whatever shade exists, and let her drink water slowly
options.consequence: Rest and fluids often improve heat exhaustion. Monitor closely. If confusion develops, descend fast.
considerations: Rest and water are first aid for heat exhaustion
Watch for confusion, which signals heatstroke
If she improves, walk out slowly. If worse, call for help

options.label: Walk back to the creek to cool off and rest
options.consequence: A safe choice if rest alone does not help. Cool water speeds recovery but means backtracking.
considerations: Walking back is a sensible fallback
Water and coolness help heat exhaustion
Only do this if rest alone does not improve things

payload.expertNote: Heat exhaustion shows as dizziness, weakness and nausea with sweating. Heatstroke adds confusion and dry skin. Both need rest immediately.
payload.sayThisLine: "We started at dawn because the canyon is dangerous by noon."

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: We turned back because the heat was getting serious and I was dizzy.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: She thought the heat was dangerous

payload.translation: She recognized the early signs of heat illness (dizziness) and made a smart choice to descend before it worsened.

followUps.line: Good call. Did you rest and drink water?
followUps.why: Shows you know the first aid.

followUps.line: Did you start earlier on your next trip?
followUps.why: Asks if she learned from it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Recognize that dizziness in heat is serious. Applaud the decision to turn back.

lessons.title: Going high
lessons.objective: You can explain acclimatization and recognize altitude sickness.

payload.prompt: What is altitude sickness?

options.text: Headache, nausea and fatigue from going up too fast
A cold caught at high elevation

explanation.correct: Altitude sickness happens when you climb too fast for your body to adjust. Symptoms are headache, nausea, and fatigue above roughly 8,000 feet.
explanation.incorrect: Altitude sickness is real: low oxygen causes headache, nausea and weakness.
explanation.sayThisLine: "I had a headache at the pass. Altitude, I think."

payload.prompt: What is acclimatization?

options.text: Letting your body adapt to elevation by ascending gradually

explanation.correct: Acclimatization is your body adjusting to lower oxygen over time. You do it by ascending gradually, not racing to the top.
explanation.incorrect: Acclimatization happens naturally with time. Slow ascent and sleeping at an intermediate height help.

payload.prompt: How do you acclimatize on a mountain trip to 12,000 feet?

options.text: Drive to 12,000 feet as fast as possible
Spend a night at an intermediate elevation like 8,000 or 9,000 feet first
Run at altitude to build fitness
There is no strategy, you just go

explanation.correct: Ascending slowly with stops at intermediate elevations lets your body adapt. Sleeping lower than your high point helps most.
explanation.incorrect: Going fast causes altitude sickness. A slow ascent and sleeping at intermediate heights give your body time to adjust.
explanation.sayThisLine: "We're spending a night at 8,000 feet to acclimatize first."

payload.prompt: You flew into a town at 10,500 feet yesterday and woke up with a headache, nausea and fatigue. Today you had plans to hike to 12,500 feet.

situation.narrative: You arrived last night and slept poorly with a mild headache. You feel sluggish but not terrible.

options.label: Hike anyway, you will feel better once you move
options.consequence: Climbing higher makes altitude sickness worse. You will feel worse, not better.
considerations: Going higher worsens symptoms
Your body needs time to adjust
Exercise at altitude makes it worse

options.label: Rest at this elevation today and hike tomorrow
options.consequence: Rest and time improve acclimatization. Tomorrow you will feel much better and the hike will be enjoyable.
considerations: One day of rest often solves mild symptoms
Gradual ascent works best
Tomorrow's hike will be better

options.label: Descend to a lower town and delay your hike
options.consequence: A safe choice if symptoms do not improve. Descending then returning after acclimatization works.
considerations: Descending fixes altitude sickness quickly
But rest at this elevation often works
Only descend if rest does not help or symptoms worsen

payload.expertNote: Altitude sickness is about rate of ascent. Fly in and immediately go higher and you will feel it. Rest at an intermediate elevation first.
payload.sayThisLine: "I had a headache yesterday, but after resting today I felt fine for the hike."

payload.prompt: You are planning a hike to 13,000 feet. What is smart preparation?

options.text: Fly in and hike the next day
Drive in gradually or spend time at intermediate elevations first
Just go, altitude is not a big deal

explanation.correct: Gradual ascent is the best prevention. Stop at intermediate elevations and sleep lower than your high point.
explanation.incorrect: Flying in and hiking immediately is a recipe for altitude sickness. Gradual ascent prevents it.
explanation.sayThisLine: "We drive up slowly and sleep at eight thousand first."
